questions: How many unit boxes does Mia have, and how many does Ben have?
How does the ruler prove that every unit box is the same length?
segments.say: Unit bars: every unit is the same length. Watch Mia's 2 unit boxes and Ben's 3 unit boxes slide into place, then follow the ruler as it checks that every box matches. Keep your student notes open at the unit box definition for this scene.

questions: What does the before bar show, and what does the after bar show?
Which unit moved, and where did it go?
segments.say: Before-and-after: the model shows what changed. Mia starts with 3 units, one unit moves away along the arrow to her sister, and the after bar shows 2 units left. Now try the before-and-after question on the worksheet in pairs.

questions: Why do we draw the whole bar before marking the parts?
How do we find the difference between the boys' units and the girls' units?
segments.say: Worked example: part-whole and difference. Draw the whole class bar first, split it into 7 equal units, mark 3 units as boys, and read the girls off as the other 4 units - the difference is 1 unit. Check this against the part-whole model in your student notes.

questions: What is wrong with Sam's drawing of 1 unit and 2 units?
How long should a correct 2-unit bar be, compared with the 1-unit bar?
segments.say: Watch out: bars must be to scale. Sam's unit boxes do not match, so his 2-unit bar is not twice his 1-unit bar; the correct bars underneath are exactly to scale. Finish by taking the exit ticket on your own - its first question revisits exactly this trap.
segments.watchFor: Drawing unit boxes in any lengths, guessing the sizes. Listen and look for it in pair talk and on the exit ticket: The bar is treated as a rough sketch rather than a scale model. Send them back to scene s4 and to the correct turn: Every unit box must be exactly the same length: two units is exactly twice one unit.
